name: South Korea: Seoul, Busan, Jeonju, Gyeongju, Andong, Sokcho

cities.base: Jongno or Euljiro, inside the old city wall. From there four palaces, Gwangjang, the nogari alley and the Inwangsan wall path are all on foot or one subway stop, and you are on Line 1 for Seoul Statio
cities.name: Seoul

cities.base: Nampo-dong for the first time: Jagalchi, Gukje, Bupyeong night market and Bosu-dong are one walk, and Line 1 runs north to Seomyeon and Beomeosa. Haeundae is a beach with towers and puts you 40 minute
cities.name: Busan

cities.base: Sleep in a hanok inside the village if you want the courtyard and the ondol floor, and accept a thin mattress and a shared bathroom; sleep in Gaeksa or Jungang-dong, ten minutes walk, if you want a be
cities.name: Jeonju

cities.base: Hwangnam-dong or Gyo-dong, in the old centre, so the tomb park, Cheomseongdae and Wolji are a night walk rather than a taxi. Bomun Lake is where the coach hotels are and it is 6 km out with nothing ar
cities.name: Gyeongju

cities.base: The town centre near the Old Market, so the jjimdak alley and Woryeonggyo are walkable after dark and the station is ten minutes. Everything else, Hahoe, Byeongsan, Dosan, Bongjeongsa, is 15 to 40 min
cities.name: Andong

cities.base: Sokcho town, near the Tourist and Fishery Market and the gaetbae crossing, and take bus 7 or 7-1 out to Sogongwon for 1,530 won in about 25 minutes. Sleeping at Seorak-dong puts you at the trailhead a
cities.name: Sokcho and Seoraksan

cities.base: Jungang-dong, on the harbour between the fish market and the two painted hills, so Dongpirang, Seopirang, Sebyeonggwan and the ferry terminal are all on foot. The cable car and Dara Park are on Mireuk
cities.name: Tongyeong

places.name: Gyeongbokgung
places.note: Shut Tuesdays, 3,000 won, and free if you turn up in rented hanbok, which is why half the courtyard is in rented hanbok. Go at 09:00 before the coaches and walk straight through to Gyeonghoeru and the Hyangwonjeong pond at the back, where almost nobody goes.

places.name: Changdeokgung and the Huwon
places.note: Shut Mondays. The better palace of the two: it was built to follow the hill rather than flatten it. The Huwon is a separate 5,000 won timed tour, 100 people a slot, half of those booked online three days ahead, and you cannot wander it alone. English slots are roughly 10:30, 11:30, 14:30 and 15:30.

places.name: Jongmyo Shrine
places.note: Shut Tuesdays. Weekdays are timed guided entry only; Saturdays, Sundays and the last Wednesday of the month you walk it yourself, which is the version worth having. Two very long empty halls and a gravel spirit path you are not meant to walk on. Twenty minutes of looking, an hour of quiet.

places.name: National Museum of Korea
places.note: Free, and open every weekday including Monday, which surprises people. Wednesdays and Saturdays it runs to 21:00, and the near-empty Buddhist sculpture room at 19:00 with the two pensive bodhisattvas is the best hour in Seoul. It closes the first Monday of March, June, September and December.

places.name: Leeum Museum of Art
places.note: Shut Mondays. The permanent Korean antiquities in Museum 1, the Mario Botta rotunda, are free; the combined ticket covering special shows runs to about 25,000 won. Celadon and Joseon white porcelain lit properly, which the national collections do not always manage.

places.name: Seodaemun Prison History Hall
places.note: Shut Mondays, 09:30 to 17:00 from November to February. Japanese colonial prison kept as it was, including the execution building and the underground cells. It is a hard ninety minutes and it explains more about how Koreans talk about the twentieth century than any palace will.

places.name: Gwangjang Market
places.note: The mung bean bindaetteok ground on the stone mill, yukhoe, and mayak gimbap. Food stalls run late daily; the fabric and hanbok shops upstairs mostly shut Sunday. It has been found: prices at the front row have roughly doubled and portions have shrunk, so walk to the quieter aisles at the back befor

places.name: Woo Lae Oak
places.note: Closed Mondays. Open since 1946 and the reference point for Pyongyang naengmyeon in Seoul: buckwheat noodles in cold beef broth, no sugar, no vinegar until you add it. The broth tastes of almost nothing for the first three mouthfuls and then of everything. Queue before 11:30 or after 14:00.

places.name: Hadongkwan
places.note: Closed Sundays, opens at 07:00 and shuts at 16:00 or whenever the pot is empty, whichever comes first. One thing on the menu since 1939: clear beef gomtang with brisket and tripe, rice already in the bowl, pay at the door on the way in. Breakfast, not lunch.

places.name: Jinju Hoegwan
places.note: Kongguksu, cold noodles in thick ground soybean broth, salted at the table by you. March to November only; out of season it is kimchi jjigae and pork belly and not worth the trip. Closed Sundays from October to March, and weekends end at 20:00.

places.name: Manseon Hof, Euljiro nogari alley
places.note: Plastic stools on the street, draft beer in frosted glasses, and dried young pollack grilled and torn apart with gochujang mayonnaise. Open daily to midnight. On a warm Friday the alley is four hundred people deep and you will share a table, which is the point.

places.name: Bukchon Hanok Village
places.note: The residential red zone behind Jeongdok Library is legally closed to visitors from 17:00 to 10:00, with a 100,000 won fine, because people live here and were being filmed through their windows. Come at 10:00, keep your voice down, and accept that it is one photogenic lane and a lot of signs asking

places.name: The city wall over Inwangsan
places.note: Free, unticketed, and the only place in central Seoul where you climb granite with the whole city underneath. Start at Changuimun and drop to Dongnimmun, or reverse it. Shamanist shrines at Guksadang on the way down and drummers on some mornings. Bring water; there is none on the ridge.

places.name: Noryangjin Fisheries Market
places.note: Open round the clock; the wholesale auction is roughly 01:00 to 05:00 and is the reason to come. You buy a fish downstairs, pay a room upstairs about 5,000 won a head to cut and serve it, and drink soju with it. Agree the price before they bag anything.

places.name: Ikseon-dong alleys
places.note: Skip it. A 1920s hanok block converted end to end into photo cafes with hour-long queues for a drink you will not finish. The same money and half the wait gets you an actual meal at Gwangjang ten minutes away.

places.name: N Seoul Tower observatory
places.note: Skip the paid observatory. The cable car queue plus the lift queue is routinely ninety minutes and the view from the free terrace at the base, or from Inwangsan, is the same city. Walk up through Namsan park by all means; do not buy the ticket.

places.name: Jagalchi Market
places.note: Shut the first and third Tuesday of most months, which no weekly calendar can hold, so check the day before. The outdoor rows where the jagalchi ajumma gut hagfish and grill them on the spot are better than the indoor tower. Buy fish at street level, carry it to the second floor, pay for cutting.

places.name: Gukje Market
places.note: Started as a black market on the war refugee trail in 1950 and still sells everything from screwdrivers to funeral clothes. Many stalls close the first and third Sunday. Eat the ssiat hotteok, a fried pancake split open and packed with sunflower seeds, from the stand on the Bipa Food Street corner.

places.name: Bupyeong Kkangtong Night Market
places.note: Runs nightly from about 19:30 in the covered arcade that sold American tinned goods off the docks, which is where the kkangtong, meaning can, comes from. Yubu jumeoni, grilled abalone skewers, Vietnamese rice paper rolls. Thirty stalls, all eaten standing.

places.name: Songjeong Samdae Gukbap
places.note: Open twenty four hours, every day. Dwaeji gukbap is the Busan dish: pork bone broth the colour of milk, rice, and a plate of saeujeot, buchu and ssamjang you are expected to build the bowl with yourself. Three generations of one family. Salt it yourself, they will not do it for you.

places.name: Gaegeum Milmyeon, Seomyeon branch
places.note: Milmyeon is naengmyeon rebuilt from wheat flour by northern refugees who could not get buckwheat in 1950s Busan, and it is chewier and sweeter than the Seoul version. Same alley as the gukbap house, thirty paces down. Order it mul, not bibim, the first time.

places.name: Gamcheon Culture Village
places.note: Since July 2026 the residential lanes are off limits before 09:00 and after 18:00, no fine attached but signposted and policed by residents. A refugee hillside painted in blocks of colour, and people still live in every one of those houses. Stay on the marked route and do not photograph through door

places.name: Huinnyeoul Culture Village
places.note: The other cliff village, on Yeongdo, with a single lane hung above the shipyards and the container road. Quieter than Gamcheon and the sea is actually in front of you. The concrete stair down to the seawall walk at the far end is steep and unlit after dark.

places.name: The Igidae coastal trail
places.note: 4.7 km of cliff boardwalk and rock steps from Dongsaengmal round to Oryukdo Quay, about two and a half hours at a normal pace. Gwangan Bridge and the Marine City towers the whole way across the water. Exposed and slippery in rain, and there is no shade in August.

places.name: Oryukdo Skywalk
places.note: Free glass shelf over the water at the end of the Igidae walk, with shoe covers handed out at the gate. Twenty minutes is plenty. The point is the five or six islands offshore, which change number depending on the tide, and that is where the name comes from.

places.name: Beomeosa
places.note: Free since temple admission charges were abolished in 2023. A working Jogye order monastery on the flank of Geumjeongsan, founded 678, with a one pillar gate and the Daeungjeon hall worth the climb. It runs one and two night templestays, roughly 70,000 to 90,000 won, booked through templestay.com.

places.name: Haedong Yonggungsa
places.note: A temple built onto the rocks with waves underneath it, which almost no Korean temple is, and consequently full by 10:00. Get there at 07:00 and you will have the 108 steps to yourself. Forty minutes on the 181 bus from Haeundae station and there is no fast way back at peak.

places.name: Taejongdae
places.note: Pine headland with sea cliffs at the southern tip of Yeongdo. The loop road is about 4.3 km on foot, or 4,000 won for the Danubi train that stops at the lighthouse and the observatory. Haenyeo still sell sea squirt and abalone from tubs on the rocks below the lighthouse.

places.name: Gwangalli beach and the bridge at night
places.note: The bridge lighting runs most evenings and the drone show fires on selected Saturdays at 20:00, free, from the sand. Better than Haeundae for this because the bars face the water across one road rather than six lanes. Cheap raw fish tents at the Millak end.

places.name: Bosu-dong Book Street
places.note: Forty odd secondhand bookshops in one alley, started by refugees selling salvaged books during the war. Almost everything is in Korean and that is fine; you go for the stacks to the ceiling and the smell. Several shops take an irregular Sunday off.

places.name: Busan Museum of Art
places.note: Shut Mondays, free for the permanent collection. The reason to come is the Lee Ufan wing next door, a separate low concrete building given over to one artist, which is a rare thing in Korea and holds up.

places.name: Haeundae Beach
places.note: Skip it in July and August, when it is a grid of rented parasols with no sand between them and the water is roped at chest height. Out of season it is a pleasant grey beach with towers behind it, which is not worth a trip either. Walk Dalmaji Hill above it instead.

places.name: Gyeonggijeon Shrine
places.note: 3,000 won. The Joseon founder's portrait hall and a bamboo grove behind it, and the only part of the Hanok Village that predates the 1930s. The hanbok rental crowd circles the front courtyard all day; go at 09:00 or after 17:00 in summer and the bamboo walk at the back stays empty either way.

places.name: Jeondong Catholic Church
places.note: Romanesque brick, finished 1914, built on the spot where the first Korean Catholic martyrs were executed in 1791. It is a working parish, so the nave is shut during Mass and on Sunday mornings you look from the porch. Ten minutes inside, and it is the best building in the village.

places.name: Omokdae
places.note: A short steep climb behind the village to the pavilion where Yi Seong-gye held a victory banquet in 1380 before founding the Joseon dynasty. Free, always open, and the only place you see the eight hundred tiled roofs as roofs rather than as a street. Best at dusk when the lanterns come on below.

places.name: Jeonju Hyanggyo
places.note: The Confucian school, free, and the quietest corner of the village because it is at the far end past where most people turn back. Four ginkgo trees over four hundred years old; in the last week of October the courtyard is ankle deep in yellow and every Korean drama crew in the country is there.

places.name: Pungnammun Gate
places.note: The last surviving gate of the old Jeonju wall, stranded on a traffic island now, lit at night. You look at it for five minutes on the way between the Hanok Village and Nambu Market, which is exactly what it is good for.

places.name: Gajok Hoegwan
places.note: Open since 1979 and run by a holder of the Jeonju bibimbap intangible heritage designation. Bibimbap done properly means the rice is cooked in beef broth, the hwangpomuk jelly and yukhoe go on raw, and about a dozen banchan arrive before it. Roughly 18,000 won. No fixed closing day; it fills at 12:3

places.name: Hankook Jib
places.note: The other claimant to the original Jeonju bibimbap, trading since 1952, five minutes from Gajok Hoegwan. Their version arrives in a brass bowl with the egg yolk raw on top and the sesame oil already in. Pick one of the two, not both in a day; the banchan alone will finish you.

places.name: Waengi Kongnamul Gukbap
places.note: Open twenty four hours. Bean sprout soup with rice, a raw egg dropped in a side bowl that you are meant to pour a spoon of broth over and swallow, and a shot glass of moju, spiced rice wine, alongside. It is the Jeonju hangover cure and it costs about 9,000 won. Breakfast here, bibimbap at lunch.

places.name: Veteran Kalguksu
places.note: One room, one queue, and knife-cut noodles in a thick broth finished with perilla powder and a heap of dried seaweed that looks wrong and tastes right. About 9,000 won. The mandu are the better order if the queue is long, because they hand them over faster.

places.name: Nambu Market night market
places.note: Fridays and Saturdays only, 17:00 to 23:00, all year. Roughly forty stalls set up inside the covered market: skewers, fried things, Vietnamese and Thai stands run by married-in families, and the pork jerky. If your Jeonju night is a Tuesday you have missed it, so plan the weekend around this.

places.name: Nambu Market by day
places.note: The working market under the same roof, seven hundred stalls of dried fish, sesame oil pressed while you wait, and pig trotters. Many shops take the first and third Sunday off. The Youth Mall on the second floor is a dozen small kitchens run by people in their twenties and is cheaper than anything i

places.name: Samcheon-dong makgeolli alley
places.note: You order makgeolli by the kettle, about 15,000 won, and the anju comes free and keeps coming: pajeon, steamed egg, grilled fish, boiled pork. Order a second kettle and a better round arrives. Fifteen minutes by taxi from the Hanok Village and worth leaving it for.

places.name: Jaman Mural Village
places.note: A hillside of painted house walls behind Omokdae, added as a regeneration project. Fifteen real minutes of looking and a lot of cafes charging Seoul prices for the view. Go because it is on the way down from Omokdae, not as a destination.

places.name: PNB Pungnyeon Bakery choco pie
places.note: Skip the queue. A marshmallow sandwich biscuit in a gift box that Korean tourists buy as omiyage, sold at four branches and by now in Seoul department stores. It is fine. It is not a reason to stand in the street for forty minutes in a city with this much actual food.

places.name: Bulguksa
places.note: Free since 2023. Two eighth century stone staircases and the Dabotap and Seokgatap pagodas are original Silla; the wooden halls above them are twentieth century reconstruction, which the signage does not stress. First bus of the day or you share it with school trips. Parking is 1,000 to 2,000 won.

places.name: Seokguram Grotto
places.note: Free, and behind glass, which is the disappointment nobody warns you about: the granite Buddha is sealed off for humidity control and you see it from a wooden corridor at an angle. It is still the finest single object in Korea. Walk up from Bulguksa, 3.2 km and about an hour, rather than taking the

places.name: Gyeongju National Museum
places.note: Free, open every day of the week, 10:00 to 19:00 at weekends and to 21:00 on Saturdays and the last Wednesday of the month. Go before the tombs, not after: the gold crowns and the Emile bell out in the yard are what was inside the mounds, and the mounds are empty grass without them.

places.name: Daereungwon and Cheonmachong
places.note: Twenty three grass burial mounds in a walled park, 3,000 won, and one of them, Cheonmachong, is cut open so you can walk inside to the replica coffin and crown. Open to 22:00 and lit, which is the version to take: at 20:00 it is almost empty and the mounds read properly against the sky.

places.name: Cheomseongdae
places.note: A nine metre stone bottle from the 640s, generally called the oldest surviving observatory in East Asia, standing alone in a field. Free, unfenced, and floodlit after dark. It takes ten minutes. The rapeseed in May and the cosmos in September around it are why people stay longer.

places.name: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond
places.note: 3,000 won, open to 22:00, and only worth doing after dark when three reconstructed pavilions are lit and doubled in the water. Daytime it is a pond and some foundations. Expect a crowd at the one famous reflection angle and walk two minutes further round for the same view alone.

places.name: Namsan: Samneung to Geumobong
places.note: Free and unstaffed. A pine ridge with about a hundred Buddhas carved into or out of the rock scattered up it, most of them unsigned and unfenced, including the headless seated Buddha ten minutes above the Samneung car park. Roughly 5 km and 400 m of climb to Geumobong, four hours round. Poor footing

places.name: Gyochon Village and the Choi family house
places.note: Free. The Choi family were landlords here for twelve generations and their rule was never to hold land beyond a day's walk; the house and the granary are open. Gyodong beopju, the family rice wine, is sold on site and tasted free, and the Silla hanok street outside is newer than it looks.

places.name: Woljeonggyo Bridge
places.note: A full scale rebuild, finished 2018, of a Silla covered bridge that burned in the fourteenth century, and it is honest about being new. Free, walk across it, and at night the reflection in the Namcheon is the reason it exists. Ten minutes from Gyochon on foot.

places.name: Yangdong Folk Village
places.note: 4,000 won, UNESCO listed alongside Hahoe, and far less visited than either Hahoe or central Gyeongju. Around 160 houses on a wooded slope, most still lived in by Wolseong Son and Yeogang Yi descendants. A car or the 203 bus, which takes about 50 minutes and does not run often. Winter hours end at 17

places.name: Gyeongju ssambap on Ssambap Street
places.note: A dozen houses on one street doing the same thing: twenty odd small dishes, a basket of leaves, grilled fish, ssamjang, and you build each mouthful yourself. About 18,000 won a head with a two person minimum at most of them. Byeolchaeban Gyodong Ssambap is the one with the queue and it earns it.

places.name: Seongdong Market
places.note: Where Gyeongju actually shops, ten minutes from the tomb park and visited by almost nobody who comes for the tombs. Haejangguk, hand cut noodles, mounds of dried anchovy. Some stalls take the second and fourth Sunday. Cash is easier than card.

places.name: Golgulsa templestay and sunmudo
places.note: The cave temple that teaches sunmudo, a Buddhist martial art, and the one templestay in Korea built around it. One night runs roughly 70,000 to 90,000 won including meals; you are up at 04:00 for the bell. Book on templestay.com well ahead. Thirty five minutes from Gyeongju by car and awkward withou

places.name: Hwangnidan-gil cafes
places.note: Skip it. One lane of hanok converted into photo cafes and Gyeongju bread outlets, named after a Seoul street, and it fills the block between the tombs and the museum with queues. The tombs are forty metres away and free after dark.

places.name: Hahoe Folk Village
places.note: 5,000 won including the shuttle from the car park, 09:00 to 17:00 November to January. A Ryu clan village in a river loop, still lived in and farmed, which is why it reads differently from a reconstruction. Cross to Buyongdae cliff on the small ferry for the view that explains the shape of the place

places.name: Hahoe Byeolsingut Talnori
places.note: Free, roughly an hour, generally Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday at 14:00 from March to December, but the schedule shifts with the season so confirm with the village office the day before. A shaman rite turned into satire of monks and aristocrats, performed by villagers, and considerably rude

places.name: Byeongsan Seowon
places.note: Free, UNESCO listed, and the single best piece of Confucian architecture in the country. The Mandaeru pavilion is an open floor on pillars with no wall on the river side, so the cliff and the water are framed like a scroll. Ten minutes on a dirt road past Hahoe and almost nobody makes the turn. Clos

places.name: Dosan Seowon
places.note: Free. Yi Hwang, the scholar on the 1,000 won note, taught here and the small thatched study he actually used is behind the grander halls added after he died. On the lake road 25 km out of town, so combine it with Gunja Village rather than doing it alone. Winter closing is 17:00.

places.name: Bongjeongsa
places.note: Free. The Geungnakjeon hall is the oldest wooden building standing in Korea, dated by a roof beam inscription to a repair in 1363, which means the frame is thirteenth century. It is small, plain, and unroped. The Yeongsanam hermitage five minutes further up has a better courtyard and nobody in it.

places.name: Woryeonggyo Bridge
places.note: 387 metres of wooden footbridge over the Nakdong, built in 2003 and named for a sixteenth century widow's letter found in a grave nearby. Free, lit after sunset, with a small fountain show most evenings in warm months. Fifteen minutes walk from the folk village and the obvious thing to do after dinn

places.name: Jjimdak Alley, Andong Old Market
places.note: Eight or nine shops in one covered alley all selling the same dish, and the dish was invented right here in the 1980s, not in some Joseon kitchen. Chicken braised in soy, sugar and dried chilli with glass noodles and potato, about 30,000 won for a small, which feeds two generously. Ask for it deopge

places.name: Heotjesabap at Kkachi Gumeong Jip
places.note: Literally false ancestral rite food: the scholar families here ate the memorial dishes on ordinary days, so it is soy sauce not chilli, no garlic, steamed vegetables, grilled fish and a soup, mixed at the table in a brass bowl. About 17,000 won. Deliberately bland, and it is the only place in Korea

places.name: Andong ganggodeungeo
places.note: Salted mackerel, grilled. Andong is a hundred kilometres inland and the fish used to arrive walked over the passes from Yeongdeok, salted twice on the way to survive the trip, and the town kept eating it that way after the roads improved. Order it as a baekban and the banchan outnumber the fish six

places.name: Andong Soju and Traditional Food Museum
places.note: Free, attached to the working distillery, closed Sundays and over the New Year. Andong soju is 45 percent and distilled from rice, nothing like the green bottle: a small tasting is included and a 400 ml bottle is about 20,000 won. Half an hour, and it explains why the local drinking is different.

places.name: Ogyeon Gunja Village
places.note: Free. The Gwangsan Kim clan's houses, moved uphill in the 1970s when the Andong dam flooded the old site, now looking over the reservoir. Twenty houses, hardly any visitors, and several take paying guests for the night. Ten minutes from Dosan Seowon so do the two together.

places.name: Imcheonggak
places.note: A 1519 scholar house, birthplace of Yi Sang-ryong, who sold it to fund the independence army in Manchuria. The Japanese drove the railway through the middle of the compound on purpose; the track was finally lifted in 2020 and the missing wings are being rebuilt. Free, and you can stay the night in i

places.name: Jebiwon Seokbul, the standing Buddha
places.note: A twelve metre Goryeo Buddha whose body is carved into a natural granite boulder with a separately cut stone head set on top, which is a thing only this part of Korea did. Free, unstaffed, twenty minutes from the station, and you will be alone with it.

places.name: Ulsanbawi
places.note: Free since the 3,500 won temple heritage charge was abolished. 7.6 km round from Sogongwon with about 670 m of climb, four to five hours, and the last 1.5 km is over 800 steel steps bolted to the rock. No reservation, no cap, so in the third week of October it is a standing queue on the stairs. Rang

places.name: Biseondae and Geumganggul
places.note: Flat 2.3 km along the granite stream bed to Biseondae, then an optional 600 m of near-vertical steel ladder to the Geumganggul cave shrine. Do the flat part in an hour with anybody; do the ladder only if stairs do not frighten you. This is the fallback when Ulsanbawi is iced or queueing.

places.name: Gwongeumseong by the Seorak cable car
places.note: 16,000 won return, same day counter sales only because they cancel on wind, so you queue in person and take the next free slot. Five minutes up to about 700 m, then a short scramble on bare rock to the fortress remains. On an autumn Saturday the wait is two hours; on a Tuesday it is twenty minutes.

places.name: Sinheungsa and the bronze Buddha
places.note: Free. Founded 653 and claimed as the oldest Seon temple anywhere; the 14.6 m seated bronze at the entrance is from 1997 and everyone photographs that instead. Walk past it to the actual halls under the cliff. It is on the way to every Seoraksan trailhead so it costs you nothing to include.

places.name: Daecheongbong by the Osaek route
places.note: The 1,708 m summit, and the Osaek side is the short brutal way: 5 km up, 1,300 m of gain, five hours climbing and three down, no water past the first kilometre. Gates open around 03:00 in summer and later in winter, and rangers enforce a turnaround time. Crampons are required from December to March

places.name: Sokcho Tourist and Fishery Market
places.note: Open daily, busiest 17:00 to 20:00. Squid sundae, fried crab, sweet fish cakes, and the dakgangjeong stands with the longest queues in Gangwon; the Manseok one is the famous name and there are three shops within fifty metres doing the same thing with no queue. Cash moves faster.

places.name: Abai Village and the gaetbae hand ferry
places.note: 500 won each way on a flat steel raft pulled across the channel by hand on a cable, and you are expected to grab a hook and pull. The village was settled by refugees from Hamgyong province in 1951 and still eats their food: abai sundae, which is pig intestine stuffed with rice rather than blood, and

places.name: Daepo Port
places.note: The working fishing harbour with the raw fish tanks and the fried food row behind it. A hoe platter runs 40,000 to 70,000 won for two; snow crab sets start around 65,000 a head and are the expensive trap. The cheaper move is the fried squid and prawn stands at the front for about 12,000 won.

places.name: Yeonggeumjeong
places.note: A pavilion on a rock stack joined to the shore by a footbridge, and the standard Sokcho sunrise. Free and always open. Ten minutes of looking, and the point is that Seoraksan is behind you and the East Sea in front in the same turn of the head.

places.name: Naksansa
places.note: Free, 20 minutes south. Founded 671, burned to the ground in the 2005 Yangyang fire and rebuilt; the 16 m white stone Haesugwaneum above the sea survived and is the reason to come. Uisangdae pavilion on the cliff edge is the better viewpoint of the two.

places.name: Mulhoe at the Jungang market end
places.note: Raw fish in iced chilli broth with pear and cucumber, eaten with a spoon, then noodles or rice dropped into what is left. About 18,000 won. It is a summer dish and a hangover dish, and half the counters here close for a day in midweek with no pattern to it, so have a second choice.

places.name: Sokcho dakgangjeong
places.note: Twice fried chicken lacquered in sweet chilli syrup, sold by the box for about 16,000 won and eaten cold on the bus back, which is how it travels. The queue at the famous stall runs an hour on Saturdays. The shops either side are the same recipe and the same oil.

places.name: Tongyeong Jungang Live Fish Market
places.note: Open daily, with the real trade before 08:00. Sea squirt, oysters from October to March, and live octopus in tanks on the quay. Pick from a tank, pay the cutting fee, carry it to a second floor room with a table. The oyster season is the one to plan for; this is where half of Korea's oysters come as

places.name: Dongpirang
places.note: A hillside of small houses due for demolition in 2007 that was saved by painting the walls, and the murals are repainted by competition every two years so it is never the same twice. Free. People live here: the signs asking for quiet before 09:00 are meant. Fifteen minutes up from the fish market.

places.name: Seopirang and the 99 steps
places.note: The west hill, opposite Dongpirang, with none of the crowd and a better view over the whole harbour and the cable car ridge behind it. Free. A piano built into the 99 steps plays when you tread on them, which is either delightful or the reason to come at dawn instead.

places.name: Tongyeong cable car to Mireuksan
places.note: 17,000 won return, 1,975 m of cable, and it shuts for maintenance on the second and fourth Wednesday of the month, which catches people out. From the top station it is a 15 minute climb to the 461 m summit and the Hallyeo archipelago laid out underneath. It closes for wind often; ring first.

places.name: Mireuksan down on foot
places.note: Ride the cable car up and walk down the Yonghwasa trail instead of queueing twice: about 3.5 km, mostly stone steps under pine, ninety minutes, and it drops you at a working temple rather than a car park. Knees, not lungs. Do not attempt it in the dark; there is no lighting.

places.name: Hansando and Jeseungdang
places.note: Twenty five minutes on the ferry from Tongyeong passenger terminal, around 15,000 won return, then a 20 minute walk to Jeseungdang, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's headquarters during the 1592 war and the site of the crane wing formation. Boats are cancelled in heavy weather and the last one back leaves earlie
places.neighborhood: Hansan-myeon, by ferry from the passenger terminal

places.name: Ttungbo Halmae Gimbap
places.note: Open every day from 06:00. Chungmu gimbap is rice rolled plain in seaweed with the squid and radish kimchi served separately, because sailors packing lunch for a hot boat learned the filling spoils inside the roll. About 8,000 won. Tongyeong was called Chungmu, which is where the name comes from.

places.name: Sebyeonggwan
places.note: A 1605 naval headquarters hall, and one of the three largest single storey wooden buildings left in Korea, sitting almost unvisited three streets up from the fish market. 2,000 won. Take your shoes off and stand in the middle of the floor; the scale only registers from inside.

places.name: Nammangsan Park
places.note: A wooded headland at the end of the harbour with a sculpture park, a statue of Yi Sun-sin and an unbroken view back over the boats. Free, always open, twenty minutes on foot from the market. Locals walk it after dinner and almost no visitor does.

places.name: Dara Park and the Dallanggil coast road
places.note: The 23 km loop road round the south of Mireuk island, with Dara Park at the far end looking over a scatter of islands that turn black at sunset. You need a car or a taxi; the bus is infrequent and drops you a long way from the viewpoint. Free, and the best hour of the day in Tongyeong.

places.name: Tongyeong ssambap and haemul ttukbaegi
places.note: The southern version of the wrapped meal, built on seaweed and shellfish rather than beef: about twenty dishes, a pot of seafood stew, and leaves. Roughly 20,000 won a head with a two person minimum. Several of the houses behind the market take a rotating midweek day off, so ask at the first door be

places.name: Tongyeong kkulppang
places.note: Skip the queue at the famous shop. A deep fried red bean doughnut glazed in syrup, sold by about thirty bakeries within four streets, all of them adequate and none of them different. Buy one from whichever door has nobody at it and spend the forty minutes on Seopirang.

outings.why: 7.6 km round and 670 m up to a granite fin above the whole range, and the last 1.5 km is more than 800 steel steps bolted onto rock. The hard part is not the climbing, it is that there is no cap on numbers: in mid October you queue on the s
outings.name: Ulsanbawi
outings.season: All year. Crampons December to March. Avoid the last three w
outings.fallback: Biseondae, flat along the stream bed, an hour each way with no stairs.

outings.why: The 1,708 m summit, and Osaek is the short steep way: 5 km and 1,300 m of gain, five hours up and three down, with no water past the first kilometre. Rangers open the gate around 03:00 in summer and enforce a turnaround time, so a late star
outings.name: Daecheongbong by the Osaek route
outings.season: May to October without crampons. December to March they chec
outings.fallback: Gwongeumseong on the cable car and the Biseondae flat, which is the whole valley in four hours.

outings.why: Two easy kilometres along polished granite slabs in the stream bed, then an optional 600 m of steel ladder up the cliff to a cave shrine. The flat section suits anybody; the ladder does not suit anyone afraid of exposure.
outings.name: Biseondae and Geumganggul
outings.fallback: Stop at Biseondae, turn round, and put the afternoon into the Sokcho fish market.

outings.why: A pine ridge with roughly a hundred Silla Buddhas carved into the rock up its flanks, unsigned, unfenced and mostly unvisited, which is the opposite of Bulguksa in every way. About 5 km and 400 m of climb. Wet granite is treacherous and the
outings.name: Namsan: Samneung to Geumobong
outings.season: All year; avoid after heavy rain.
outings.fallback: Walk the first twenty minutes to the headless seated Buddha and turn back, then Gyochon and Woljeonggyo.

outings.why: Both free since 2023. The 3.2 km forest path from the temple up to the grotto takes about an hour and is the only way to arrive at Seokguram the way it was meant to be reached. The grotto itself is behind glass, which is worth knowing befor
outings.name: Bulguksa and the walk up to Seokguram
outings.fallback: Bus 12 up to Seokguram and walk down, which halves the climbing.

outings.why: 160 clan houses on a wooded slope 25 km north, still lived in, and visited by a fraction of the numbers Hahoe gets. 4,000 won. The 203 bus takes about 50 minutes and does not run often, so check the return time before you walk in.
outings.name: Yangdong Village
outings.fallback: Gyochon Village and the Choi house in the old centre, free, for an hour.

outings.why: 5,000 won and the shuttle, a lived-in Ryu clan village in a bend of the Nakdong, plus the free mask dance at 14:00 on most Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays from March to December. Confirm the performance day with the village offic
outings.name: Hahoe Village and the 14:00 talnori
outings.season: Mask dance roughly March to December.
outings.fallback: Byeongsan Seowon ten minutes away, free, and the better building anyway.

outings.why: The best Confucian architecture in Korea and the oldest wooden building in Korea, both free, both under-visited, 40 minutes apart. The problem is transport: the Byeongsan road is dirt and the buses are rare, so this is a hire car or a half-
outings.name: Byeongsan Seowon and Bongjeongsa
outings.season: All year. Both close 17:00 November to January.
outings.fallback: Bongjeongsa alone, which has a regular bus from Andong station.

outings.why: Yi Hwang's academy on the lake road 25 km north, and the Gwangsan Kim houses moved uphill when the dam flooded their village, ten minutes further. Both free and both nearly empty. One bus an hour and the last one back is early.
outings.name: Dosan Seowon and Ogyeon Gunja Village
outings.fallback: Imcheonggak and the Jebiwon Buddha, both within 20 minutes of Andong station.

outings.why: 4.7 km of cliff boardwalk and rock steps from Dongsaengmal round to Oryukdo Quay, about two and a half hours, with Gwangan Bridge across the water the whole way. Exposed, no shade, and the rock steps are slick in rain.
outings.name: The Igidae coastal trail to Oryukdo
outings.fallback: Huinnyeoul on Yeongdo, a flat hour above the shipyards, then the seawall.

outings.why: The fish market while it is still working, the war refugee market behind it, and the covered night arcade, all within 600 metres. Jagalchi shuts the first and third Tuesday of most months and many Gukje stalls take the first and third Sunda
outings.name: Jagalchi at seven, then Gukje and Bupyeong
outings.season: All year. Oysters and hagfish are best October to March.
outings.fallback: Bosu-dong Book Street and the ssiat hotteok stand, which are open when the markets are not.

outings.why: Twenty five minutes on the ferry, around 15,000 won return, then a short walk to Yi Sun-sin's 1592 headquarters above the bay where he destroyed the Japanese fleet. Sailings stop in heavy weather and the last boat back is earlier than the t
outings.name: Hansando and Jeseungdang
outings.fallback: The cable car up Mireuksan and the Yonghwasa path down.

outings.why: 17,000 won return but buy one way, ride up, climb fifteen minutes to the 461 m summit over the Hallyeo islands, then take the Yonghwasa stone steps down. The cable car shuts the second and fourth Wednesday of the month and closes on wind wi
outings.name: Mireuksan by cable car, down on foot
outings.season: All year. Call ahead on windy days.
outings.fallback: Dongpirang, Seopirang and Sebyeonggwan on foot from the market.

outings.why: Changuimun to Dongnimmun along the restored wall and over bare granite, with the whole city underneath and shaman shrines at Guksadang near the bottom. Free and unticketed. No water on the ridge and the granite slabs are dangerous when wet.
outings.name: The Seoul City Wall over Inwangsan
outings.fallback: The Naksan section on the east side, half the climb and all of it paved.

outings.why: All four are open and lit until 22:00 and all four are within a two kilometre walk of each other, which is the only time of day they are not full of school groups. Total ticket cost about 6,000 won. Flat, easy, and the best three hours in t
outings.name: Gyeongju after dark: Daereungwon, Cheomseongdae, Woljeonggyo, Wolji
outings.fallback: The same circuit at 09:00, which is quiet again but without the lighting.

destination.name: South Korea: Seoul, Busan, Jeonju, Gyeongju, Andong, Sokcho
destination.pitch: Ten days buys you the best eating country in Asia for the money, a granite range you can climb from a fishing town, and a Confucian and Silla heartland that most people skip because the KTX makes Seoul and Busan too easy.
destination.caveat: The two weeks of autumn colour on Seoraksan and the two of cherry blossom are when the whole country moves at once, trains sell out a month ahead and the Ulsanbawi stairs become a standing queue; outside those windows July and August are 30 degrees at 85 percent humidity with the monsoon on top, and Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: Seoul is twenty five million people with five palaces inside the old wall, a granite ridge walk at the top of it, and street drinking on plastic stools until two in the morning.
because.food: Regional and cheap and still done by families: pork bone gukbap in Seomyeon at four in the morning, bean sprout soup in Jeonju at six, a twenty dish ssambap table in Gyeongju for fourteen dollars, and memorial-rite food in Andong that exist
because.nature: Seoraksan gives you 1,300 metres of granite climbing straight out of a town with a fish market in it, and the Igidae and Hallyeo coasts are cliff walking with islands offshore rather than beach.
because.culture: Silla gold in Gyeongju, Joseon Confucianism intact at Byeongsan and Dosan, a mask dance still performed by the villagers who inherited it, and colonial and war history that the museums do not soften.
because.adventure: Daecheongbong from Osaek is 1,300 metres of gain in five kilometres with a ranger-enforced turnaround, and winter on that ridge needs crampons.
because.relaxation: Templestays at Beomeosa and Golgulsa, jjimjilbang in every town for about ten dollars, and a makgeolli alley where the food keeps arriving free as long as you keep ordering kettles.
because.exploration: Seven bases in a country the size of Indiana, all linked by trains that leave every twenty minutes and arrive to the minute, so you can change your mind at breakfast and still be somewhere else by lunch.
